newsitem.title: USA: Dupont Merck mammogram adjunct wins FDA nod.
newsitem.headline: Dupont Merck mammogram adjunct wins FDA nod.

text.p: DuPont Pharma Radiopharmaceuticals said Tuesday the U.S. Food and Drug Administration had approved a nuclear medicine test to be used as a diagnostic adjunct for patients whose mammograms are inconclusive.

The division of DuPont Merck Pharmaceutical Company said the FDA had authorized it to market Miraluma, which it described as the first nuclear medicine test approved for breast imaging and detection of breast cancer.

The Miraluma test uses an imaging agent thought to accumulate in areas of increased metabolic activity in malignant cells, the company said, with the concentration of the drug up to nine times higher in malignant cells than in normal cells.
Patients receive a small amount of the radiopharmaceutical by injection, after which the breasts are imaged with a gamma camera. Total test time is between 45 minutes and one hour, the company said.
"It is specifically an adjunct to mammography for those women who have abnormal or inconclusive mammograms," a Dupont Merck spokeswoman said.
She said the National Cancer Institute estimates as many as 30 million women have mammograms done each year, with about 11 percent needing further testing or followup because of inconclusive results.
"Miraluma will be appropriate for many of those inconclusive patients," she said, adding mammograms were particularly difficult to interpret with high breast density.
"This test is an adjunct to mammography that produces striking pictures of lesions even in the midst of difficult to image breast tissue," the company said in a prepared statement.
The DuPont Merck Pharmaceutical Company, headquartered in Wilmington, Del., is a partnership between DuPont Co and Merck & Co Inc -- marketing its products under the DuPont Pharma name.
